title: The political polarization of health outcomes in the USA
one_line: Using individual-level Add Health biomarker data, CDC death records and a 2024 opinion survey, Elder and O'Brian show conservative Americans' health and mortality diverged from liberals' during the 2010s-2020s, only half explained by demographic sorting.
key_claims: In Add Health Wave 4 (2008-2009) equivalence testing showed no significant comorbidity difference across the political spectrum, but by Wave 5 (2016-2018) the most conservative respondents had a significantly worse comorbidity index (0.305), a gap of about one-third of a standard deviation.
The comorbidity index combined five objectively measured in-home biomarkers: BMI, lipids, HbA1c, blood pressure and C-reactive protein.

Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition attributed roughly half the widening gap to demographic/socioeconomic sorting (education, income, insurance gains in the liberal coalition), outweighing conservatives' relative gains in marriage and religiosity.

Linking the cohort to the National Death Index (2020-2022), very conservative respondents were 1.144 percentage points more likely to die of internal causes than very liberal respondents; the gap persisted after excluding COVID-19 deaths and with county fixed effects.

The 2024 CHIP 50 survey (n > 21,000) found right-leaning respondents reported lower trust in primary care and ER physicians, lower willingness to seek care for an angina-like chest pain vignette, and, among the 38% with chronic illness, more doubt about the safety and effectiveness of their own medications (Beliefs about Medicines Questionnaire).
limitations: Roughly half of the widening comorbidity gap remains unexplained by observable characteristics in the decomposition.
The medical-trust mechanism is supported only by cross-sectional 2024 opinion data, not linked to the same individuals' biomarkers or deaths, so it is consistency evidence rather than causal.
The cohort is narrow in age (born roughly 1977-1982, in their early-to-mid 40s during mortality follow-up), where deaths are rare, limiting generalisability to other age groups.
Political ideology is self-reported and can change over time, making it hard to separate individual-level deterioration from coalition membership turnover.
County fixed effects address local jurisdiction but cannot rule out unmeasured individual-level confounders such as occupation or health behaviours not captured.
open_questions: Does declining medical trust prospectively predict worse biomarkers and mortality within the same individuals, rather than being inferred from a separate survey?
Would an intervention that restores clinical trust or increases care-seeking among conservative patients close any of the unexplained mortality gap?
What accounts for the unexplained half of the comorbidity divergence beyond income, education, marriage and religiosity?
Does the same divergence appear in other age cohorts and in more recent waves of mortality data?
